strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.11.a: Siuda laughed, “Oh sure, at least for a little while.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.12.desc:
Siuda looked to Valenteev, and then to the hoards of protestors that had formed the walls around him. The last thing this powder keg needed was a spark. Siuda shrugged, and smiled to the man, “What can I help you with?”

Siuda had come to know the names of the six representatives rather quickly. Each group wanted something of the other, as is only natural during negotiations, with Siuda acting as the mediator. As the chants from the people grew louder all around them, the six men struggled to iron out a deal that left everyone happy, and the city intact.

“Well that's the point of an assembly,” Siuda explained, running off of minimal sleep and diminishing hope, “each person gets one vote. If you turnout, your vote will count, simple as that. There is no way to maintain a system of anarchism with parties.” Debate erupted as the six men stumbled over top of each other to prove why the statement was true. Whatever they were trying to accomplish, it clearly wasn't working. Siuda massaged his temples intensely, trying to work out the migraine that grew and grew. The stomping of feet and constantly repeating chants made Siuda yearn for the Black Army to simply intervene, to create a path and let all six protest groups march as they chose and everyone could go home.

Three hours had passed.

By then, the chants had died out, and now, the negotiations were more an exhibit, or rather, an inverted zoo. Six crowds, six beasts, stood around the seven humans and watched as they murmured and mumbled. Finally, one of them stepped back, resigning from the endurance test they had undertaken. Eight minutes later another did too, and one more, and two more, and then it was just Siuda and one other. “You've made your point clear on politics, and it is apparent your mind will never change and your opinions won't budge. That's fine.” said the last one standing. “I cannot, though, allow your economic policies to drive this city, and Russia at large, into the ground. There must be some compromise here or there will be no choice but to organize a general strike.” Siuda, exhausted and eager to return home, learned an important lesson,
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.12.a: Sometimes you just gotta say yes.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.13.desc:
A strict curfew had been enforced since the attacks. Rodzavesk was a city under lockdown. For good reason, of course, Abakumov wasn't taking any chances. For that, he was commendable. His first mistake though, was trying to force an anarchist to abide by the rules.

Siuda slipped out of his door and into the dead of night with nothing more than his fur coat wrapped around him. He wasn't even sure what he was hoping to find. A clue? Footprints? A giant neon sign pointing him towards the individual or group behind the attack? Any would've been nice. Instead, Siuda got the freezing rain, and pitch black city. This was stupid, he decided, come on! He turned on his heel, looking back to the trail he had made, and tried to fit his foot perfectly into the holes. When he couldn't fit into the first hole, he paid it no mind. When the second didn't, it was cause for suspicion. When Siuda looked up and saw that the footprints led the opposite way from which he came, he knew.

Siuda crept to the outskirts of the city, towards the tall trees that the buses, those damn buses, had entered from. The footsteps led further north, and Siuda followed closely behind like a loyal dog. Without explanation, the footsteps stopped. There simply were holes, and then there were not. Siuda inched closer to investigate and as he did, he heard the most peculiar sound. The ground beneath him meowed.

Siuda shook his head, clearly he had lost the plot, men didn't vanish leaving nothing but footsteps behind them, and the ground did not meow. Siuda shifted his weight to make his way back to his residence when he heard it again. A meow. Siuda furrowed his brow and looked all around him, but no source could be found. He stepped, and he heard it again. Siuda's eyes became wide with the realization; a cat could be buried in the snow! He began frantically wiping away at the thick layers of snow, until he found it.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.13.a: Not a cat, but a door.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.14.desc:
Pyotr Siuda, Yevgeniya Tarauta, Abakumov, and the other members of the Emergency Anti-Fascist Comittee gathered around in a circle on the outskirts of town. Taratuta shot Siuda a skeptical glance, “Pyotr...If you want to return back to Kansk, I'm sure that-”

“No.” He insisted, “I'm telling you, I was out late at night, and I heard this meowing, like, as if there were a cat right beneath my feet!” The members of the committee exchanged glances that conveyed emotions between concern and frustration. “I know it sounds stupid, but I'm not kidding! Look, you'll believe me when you see this,” Siuda bent down to the ground and brushed away the freshly fallen snow. Just beneath it, a wooden door, akin to one attached to a cellar, revealed itself. “I haven't opened it, the people here have entrusted you all with this responsibility, and I do as well. Whoever killed those people is behind that door.” The unlikely group exchanged glances once more, this time concern had shifted to fear and frustration to courage.

“Well,” said Abakumov, gun grapsed tightly in his hand, “unless you are planning on waiting for an invitation, I think it's time we put an end to this.”

It was decided that Siuda, Taratuta, and Abakumov would go in alone, with the other members remaining outside to maintain the continuity of the committee should the worst befall them. The trio crept quietly through the door and into a rat's maze. A labyrinth of twisting tunnels spiraled out of every wall, forking and forking again. “No shit...” Abakumov muttered under his breath, “these tunnels lead everywhere...” The three stopped at the first tunnel, where a faint light illuminated the side of the wall. The three shared looks, a silent deliberation, before Abakumov nodded his head towards the light and the three traveled down.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.14.a: They would not rest until they got to the bottom of it.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.15.t: In the Belly of the Beast
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.15.desc:
They had hardly stepped foot into the system of tunnels, when the shadow appeared against the wall. Abakumov pressed a finger against his lips and silently instructed them to tread carefully. Abakumov readied this weapon, as the shadow grew larger and larger.

Tail swaying from side to side, a gray cat sauntered past the three as if it were an average occurrence for three strangers to intrude into his home. Abakumov laughed under his breath, “It was only a ca-”

A hand pulled him off balance and around the corner. Siuda and Taratuta stumbled backwards. Yevgeniya fumbled with her gun, trying to get a grip on it, but it was too late. A bald man, scruff covering his face, stepped around the corner. He wasn't alone, held tightly against his neck was Abakumov. His eyes told a story of horror, as if he had seen a ghost. The bald man pressed the gun against his hostage's head, forcing it into the cradle between the skull and the spine. “Put your fucking gun down,” he barked, gesturing to Taratuta, “Throw it on the ground!”

Yevgenyia and Siuda shared a nervous look, before Siuda nodded, and Taratuta set her gun slowly down on the ground. Convinced he could talk his way out of it, Siuda began his usual speechisms, but the words hung heavy in his mouth. Where had he seen that bald head? That scruffy beard...Taratuta was the first to speak, “Who are you?” She demanded.

Abakumov struggled against his restraints in a futile attempt to warn his comrades who they had stumbled across. The bald man's grip tightened, “Anarchists. That's what you call yourselves? Smear Judeo-Bolshevism in shit, the result is still the same. The Vozhd warned us this day would come. If only we were more vigilant, or more thorough in our execution, we would be standing in opposite positions.”

“You...you were on the bus.” Siuda finally fumbled out, “You sat with them! You made yourself at home here! Who are you?”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.15.a: “I am the next Vozhd of all Russia.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.16.desc:
The future of the Far East would be decided underground. Pyotr Siuda, his back to the wall, and his closest confidant, Yevgeniya Taratuta, ordered to remain still, watched helplessly as their friend Abakumov struggled against the burly arms of the Ghost of Rodzaevsky. “I am the next Vozhd of all Russia,” He boasted, relishing in the pride of the sentence, “You corralled all the animals, and for that I am grateful for the stupidity of Bolsheviks. We won't all leave here.”

As the pretender Vozhd monologued, the wheels had begun to spin in Taratuta's head on just how to escape this situation with Abakumov's life. She looked back to her gun, but she had already discarded it, reaching for it now would prompt Little Hitler to react. To her left, Siuda had a completely different reaction, attempting to craft a monologue of his own to sway the ardent fascist. It seemed as if they were at a deadlock.

No history book would ever believe that the face of Russian anarchism was saved by a feline underground, yet, in context it made perfect sense. The cat returned, and began to purr, rubbing his head against the pretender Vozhd's leg. He made some effort to shoo away the cat, but hesitated. Abakumov seized the opportunity, and twisted himself free from his captor. In one fluid motion, Taratuta retrieved her gun, aimed, and made the world a little bit better.

They stopped for a moment to catch their breath, and to process what happened. Abakumov massaged his throat, “Come here. Look,” he pointed, “That wasn't a fascist, that was second in command to Rodzaevsky.” Taratuta and Siuda rounded the corner Abakumov had been snatched behind, and saw candles lit around a portrait of Rodzaevsky stacked on top of books of hate.

Siuda, still shaken by the fact he was face to face with a mad man as he got off of the bus, as a refugee no less, shook his head, “This tells me we have a long way to go before agents of hate are driven from Russia.” Taratuta offered no words, reloading her gun silently.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.16.a: She fired one bullet into the portrait, and then six more.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.17.desc:
Chita was truly a sight to behold, at least for Siuda that is. In all his days, in all his time on earth, after all he had been through, he had never expected there to still be those in Russia who would cling to the last crippled vestiges of a movement that had not bared its fangs in decades. Monarchists, hundreds of them, roaming the streets, their loyalties still rooted in the long dead name of a line that had once stained his homeland with grievous oppression. Less flabbergasted at such a thing however, was his trusted foreign minister.

“It's like I've gone backwards comrade, it really feels that way.” Siuda commented rather bluntly, his eyes still wide in disbelief as he strolled between the desolate corridors of the Tsar's once populated palace, its halls decorated with ornate fixtures and portraits of royalty forgotten by time. His companion did nothing but chuckle, a smile curling up her face as she gestured forward to the grand chamber positioned before them.

“Oh, don't blabber too much, of course places like this still exist, Harbin was always a haven for these lot and their nostalgia,” she playfully retorted, attempting to subdue his perplexed wonder and once more foster a focus toward their goal. “You asked for a suitable place, no? I believe I've delivered?”

Pyotr felt a light flicker on in his brain, a devious idea forming as he gazed upon the imperial opulence stretched far into the back corner of the rather expansive room. He could see it now, spread out chairs and desks, debate and chatter bringing life back to the abandoned structure, it would be a local assembly, it must be. The Tsar and his ways would cease to exist, trampled by the march of equality and progress, and he wouldn't have it any other way. “Yes, my friend, I believe you have.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.17.a: The past falls away, the future pushes forward.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.18.desc:
Disgust, that was the only feeling that could ever possibly adequately describe the churning nausea that Siuda felt welling up within his stomach as he leered out upon the revolting construction at the center of Amur. It was almost like it burned his eyes to look upon it, the shape a representation of all he had come to find despicable about the horrid conditions of Amur, and equally a symbol of those who had once ruled here. To call him mortified that the gigantic neon swastika was still standing, let along brimming with light that projected a harsh silhouetted glare upon the streets below, would be a dramatic understatement.

He had already decided what he wanted to do, turning to the man next to him, mumbling in shock and surprise, “Why is that still here? I want it gone within the hour, or I'll blast it to pieces myself.” Pyotr Siuda sneered, gesturing for the messenger to scurry off to the local garrison, hoping that they would arrange suitable methods to obliterate such a flagrant display of the scourge that had haunted Russia.

It was not less than thirty minutes when his message bore fruits, several men arriving, their faces hardened from the bitter siberian air. Instructions followed, charges set and a gathering amassed. In Siuda's mind doing this publicly and with definite purpose was the only way, showing the people of Amur that they were liberated, now more than ever, was his top priority. Nothing sent a message, like a few well placed explosives, and a whole lot of cheering.

Satisfaction, that would now be the descriptor for his mood, a smile overtaking his dreary expression as the queasy spasms from his midsection faded into a deep content. The people seemed happy enough, their faces dotted with wide grins and exhilarated joy, some even on the verge of tears as the monument to their oppressor was cast off with a bang, only dust in the wind.

However, some in the crowd didn't seem all that impressed, no, they seemed angry that they had dared defile the monument to the Vozhd and all he stood for. He could see them, weaving their way between the crowds as if just another batch of elated spectators, their expressions betraying their ill thought out disguise. And as he raised his hand, pointing wordlessly into the crowd, the soldiers beside him understood, stepping forward to question the new arrivals.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.19.t: By the People, For the People
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.19.desc:
Magadan was always a bit out of the way, even for a Siberian city - and this time of year, it was certainly frigid. Pyotr Siuda wouldn't've found himself here under any normal circumstance, but he was in the area, and word had gotten up that an American cargo ship had just come in a day ago, recently after the liberation of the city.

Stepping down paved roads towards the docks, an elected officer by the name of Burakh shadowed Siuda. His men had been watching the cargo ship that had docked itself in one of Magadan's jetties. By a ramp leading to the deck of the ship itself, a pair of soldiers stood next to what Siuda could only assume was the Captain of the cargo ship. He looked up as Siuda approached, and even looked a little relieved to see him.

“Finally,” the Captain grumbled in a thick accent. “Are you in charge? Should I get a translator?”

Siuda stopped in front of him. Immediately, he spoke. “Translator? No. No. No need,” He said, English tenuous.

The Captain blinked, bushy brows furrowing together. “-well, alright. We've got foodstuffs, warm clothes, lotsa' supplies for the winter here...” He explained, while Siuda nodded along. Pyotr stole a glance with Burakh, trying to hide a mischievous smile that began to creep onto his face. Siuda whispered to the young officer, murmuring an order - and just like that, Burakh peeled off, starting to marshal his men. The Captain watched as soldiers in dark uniforms started to march by.

Suffice to say, the Captain had grown more than a little suspicious. His eyes narrowed. “You are - you are the-”

Siuda cut him off. “Yes,” he responded, not even giving the Captain a chance to respond. The American looked over his shoulder as soldiers started to swarm the decks of his ships, working together to lift boxes and cart them down towards a forming crowd. The Captain looked as if he was about to protest, as soldiers broke open the crates and tossed the goods inside to beckoning civilians. Looking back at Siuda's face, and the guilty smile wrought upon it, the Captain concluded one thing.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.19.a: “I don't get paid enough for this...”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.20.desc:
Stepping up to the podium on a stage in the middle of Irkutsk, Siuda glanced upon a weary crowd that was still forming. Passing workers, men and women alike, some with children in hand, start to cluster up to be in earshot of Siuda's microphone. He wasn't nervous. Pyotr had done this many times before, but he couldn't remember the last time the crowd in a place like Kansk was so dour.

In the months since the liberation of Irkutsk, the city had undergone changes under the communes. Ripping out the ugly facets of Yagoda police state took time, and instability had grown rife as the local administration hammered out the kinks. Gripping the edge of the podium, Siuda cleared his throat and held his head high as he began to speak.

“Comrades of Irkutsk!” Siuda's voice boomed. “It has been some months since this city has been liberated from the clutches of the old Union's withering hands, and the Presidium toppled. The tyrant Yagoda - a Mussolini painted red, who would've seen you all monitored and controlled like obedient slaves by his NKVD, has been cast down and justly punished for his crimes. Now, more than ever, the future of Irkutsk looks ever brighter.”

Siuda's voice had all the charisma, the fiery quality that inspired rousing cheers all over the Angarsk river basin, but that day, it fell on deaf ears. As his eyes scanned the crowd, faces twisted into sneers, frowns - or worse yet, remained blank expressions, as if they weren't listening at all. Siuda gulped.

Perhaps they were too used to Yagoda's iron fist - like cattle, or men in the cave who had seen only the shadows. Siuda could blame them, but something deep down within him, something etched behind those weary faces, told him that it wasn't their fault. As much as it turned his stomach to admit, Yagoda's regime brought security that the Black Army hadn't. Not yet - although, it would.

Easing it back, Siuda felt his chest empty of breath. The fiery plan for his speech dissipated. He didn't know what to say next.

Taking a deep breath, he glanced upon the crowd again.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.20.a: “-and we'll have more town halls, to discuss and remedy issues you've been seeing in this city.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.21.t: The Hunt for a Black October
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.21.desc:
Pyotr Siuda stood, center of the stage in the Ulan-Ude town hall, where many ideologues and speakers like him had sat before. The auditorium was packed full of people - native Buryats, young soldiers wearing tattered uniforms, mothers and fathers, huddled close together and looking up at Siuda, on stage.

For the last hour or so of the town hall, Siuda had been doing well in answering the questions. The crowd was receptive and understanding, perhaps softened to the free nature of the Black Army by Sablin's policies. There were the standard questions about how everything'd work, what their new schedules would be, how their farms would operate, but - Siuda had done this before, in countless other cities. He didn't think Ulan-Ude would be any different.

A young woman, near the front of the crowd, raised her hand. Siuda pointed her out, and her chirpy voice filled the auditorium.

“What do you think of Comrade Sablin's past policies - and will yours be a continuation of them?”

And for the first time in the first Ulan-Ude town hall, Siuda grew silent. His eyes affixed on the woman who asked that question, and for the first time, the crowd watched the man visibly contemplate a question.

“Comrade Sablin,” drumming his fingers against the wood of the podium, “-a man of fierce ideological conviction. His message of liberation was admirable, but that much power should not sit with one man.” The crowd stared at him expectantly, but - what more could Siuda say, without complimenting a statist? Granted, he was one of the better ones.

“What about Comrade Sablin's education and literacy programmes, for our female comrades?” Another voice called out.

Siuda cleared his throat. “I can assure you, we will be continuing these policies, if not even expanding them.” His dance around the topic of Sablin seemed more precarious by the second.

“What did you think of Comrade Sablin himself!? He wasn't so different, was he?” A third voice called out. Siuda deeply sighed.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.22.desc:
There were a few rhythmic knocks on the door to Siuda's provisional office - a small space set up in what used to be a school in the city of Aldan, just so recently integrated into the Free Territory's communes. Looking up, Siuda raises his voice slightly to travel through the wooden door.

“Come in!” The knob turned, and the creaky hinges gave way to a stout man wearing thick winter furs above the raiment of a religious man. Coarse gray hairs hid a ruddy red face from the cold, and he trails in soft powdery snow from outside. “Comrade Kain! Sit, sit,” Pyotr urged.

Father Kain had a smile on his face as he settled into a stiff wooden chair across from Siuda's small desk. Out of the ice glazed window, Black Army trucks lay parked next to each other, beds being stocked full of goods and supplies to be travelling north to Omolon, Sakha, Kolyma - where Father Kain travelled from to see Siuda.

“Father Kain, please. I'm but a humble servant of the lord.” Siuda's eye twitched - but, the Father was an agreeable man, even more so for coming to see him like this. “I came to give you my thanks, Mister Siuda - all across Sakha, I hear talk of your goods getting to the tribes. Enough food to last us through the winter - we cannot be grateful enough,” Kain nodded.

Siuda smiled. The affirmation of the tangible good brought a warmth to his face that was enough to fight off the cold outside. Kain continued.

“Such charity is - the love of God and man, manifested uniquely in you and your helpers, Mister Siuda. God bless you.”

The mention of God again made Pyotr's eye twitch, and a certain funny feeling rose in his chest. He tensed up, shoulders coiled, but looking at Kain's happy, bearded face quelled such emotions, his hands slowly lost the taut tension in them as he relaxed himself. He could not bring himself to be mad at the Father - good is good, regardless of politics or religion.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.22.a: Good is good, regardless of politics or religion.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.23.desc:
A knock, deliberate and firm, echoed throughout the house. Moving from the kitchen to the door, Siuda dusted himself off. The Far East was nice, but Kansk would always be his home. “Comrade Kilchichakov! Welcome, please, come in!” Siuda stepped aside so as to let the man in. Responding only with a grunt, Kilchichakov entered into Siuda's home. “You can leave your coat wherever you please,” Siuda walked back to his kitchen and sat at one end of the table. A few moments later, Kilchichakov joined him.

“You'll have to excuse me if my cooking skills aren't what they used to be, I've been out for a while.” Siuda said in between bites.

“Yes, I've certainly noticed your absence, and I'm sure those in Tomsk did too,” Kilchichakov spat, “Though I suppose it isn't fair to blame you for that.” The room became quiet, save for the soft sounds of chewing. Eventually, the economist dabbed at his mouth with his napkin, and cleared his throat. “While I appreciate this gesture, I doubt that it's purely out of the kindest of your heart, though I suppose it wouldn't be out of character for you,” Kilchichakov conceded once again. “I've been in the game long enough to know that people invite me over when they need me, not when they want me.”

Siuda set down his fork, and prepared to meet his challenge. “The last time I saw you in person, comrade, was in Kansk. You stopped me on my way to an assembly meeting and told me I had to fight to find a recruit.” Siuda leaned back in his chair, crossing his arms, “And I realized then I was wrong about you.” He paused to let his words take their effect, “I thought you were a businessman. A capitalist. Your prowess with the economy convinced me of that. For that, I thought you were heartless, my greatest foe. But when you asked me to find that boy, I saw humanity. I saw that you aren't a bad person.” Siuda leaned forwards towards the table, “There'll come a time, sooner than later, where you will find yourself on one side or the other.”

“You're threatening me then?”

“No, no,” Siuda laughed, “I know you'll make the right decision, the decision that brought peace to that mother, and the decision that'll make it so it'll never happen again.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.23.a: Though he would never admit it, Kilchichakov had been convinced.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.24.desc:
Though she never had any of her own, Taratuta had always had a soft spot for children. In her eyes, more people ought to act like children. Optimistic and curious, but above all else, hopeful. She saw that hope in the eyes of the children that had formed a semi-circle around her. The Tomsk Public Library had graciously accepted her offer to showcase her proudest achievement; a children's book. The city had been scarred by the reaction to peaceful demonstrators ordered by Stepanov, but the joy of children could heal any wound.

“Ok children!” A slender woman's chipper voice bringing the children to order, “Today, we have a very special guest reader, Comrade Taratuta! What do we say to her?” A chorus of children responded with a thousand different answers ranging from greetings to expressing their desire to go to the bathroom. The woman smiled at Taratuta, rolling her eyes, “Ok! Ok, let's calm back down. We're going to be very quiet, and very respectful while she reads, ok?” Various indications of agreement came from the hoard of children. With that, Taratuta opened her storybook, and flipped to the first page.

“There once was a mouse named Georgy. Everyday, he woke up, and made his way to school.”

“Mice don't go to school!” One child cried, “I've never seen a mouse go to school!”

Taratuta smiled through the interruption, only a child would see the need to correct a fantasy. “Ah, but this is a world where they do!” The response seemed to placate the child and Taratuta was free to continue. “One day, while on the playground, Georgy had bumped into Fyodor, a huge dragon who used her size to bully all the other schoolchildren. 'Give me your lunch, little mouse!' Fyodor thundered. Georgy was scared! Fyodor could swallow him whole! Georgy reached into his backpack to hand over his lunch, when another student ran up beside him.”

Taratuta licked her finger, turning the still stuck together pages, “A girl he knew from class ran to Georgy's side, 'Stop!' She said, 'Why does she deserve your lunch? That's yours!' The girl turned to Fyodor, standing at the foot of the dragon, 'Just because you're stronger, doesn't mean you get to push us around!' The scene had attracted the attention of many of the other schoolchildren who joined her, standing beside her. 'You may be able to pick on us alone, but together, we are stronger than you!'” Taratuta gently closed the book, and smiled back at the children.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.24.a: Their smiling faces was all the reward she needed.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.25.desc:
It's never just one drink. As Stepan Valenteev and Pyotr Siuda sat idle, side by side at the bar, their conversation jumped from topic to topic sporadically. “I swear!” Siuda cackled, “I'm being completely honest! She made a doll in my likeness, out of her own hair!” Siuda put emphasis on the last words, exaggerating the absurdity of the statement. The typically stoic General Valenteev couldn't help but laugh. “And, and, and,” Siuda continued, “She asked me if I liked it!” Siuda made a face of disbelief, “Do I like it?! So what do I do? Tell her no? That it's the most disgusting thing I've ever laid eyes on? I had to tell her I loved it! I still have it in my suitcase!” The two shared a minute of pure, alcohol induced laughter.

As the laughing died down, Valenteev wiped at his eyes, “Ah Comrade Siuda-”

“Please, Pyotr would be enough.”

“You know how to have fun, I have not had a chance to unwind like this since the last time we drank together. Your invitation tonight was thoroughly appreciated.” Valenteev stood, stumbling only slightly, and pushed his stool against the bar.

Siuda rose with him, grabbing his coat from the rack adjacent, “Let me walk you to your vehicle.” He insisted, “There was one more thing I was hoping to discuss.” As the two walked out of the bar and into the cold, outside world, reality set back in. They were not friends, or comrades, or simple war buddies, they were responsible for this land. Siuda turned to Valenteev, gripping tightly on his shoulder, “Comrade. I'm afraid we won't have many more moments like this.”

Valenteev, still under the influence, flashed a dopey smile, “I would have to agree, we're almost to my car.”

Siuda offered back polite laughter, but the cold had largely sobered him up, “No, that's not quite what I mean. You know Ivan is plotting something, I feel it. The protest in Tomsk, the attack on our convoy, hell, if he pulled the strings behind the strings behind the demonstrators in Irkutsk too! He's going to act soon, Comrade. I need to know if you're on my side.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.25.a: Valenteev threw his head back in laughter, “You thought I would support Ivan?”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.26.desc:
Stepanov gently massaged at his temple with one hand and violently clenched the other. His eyes darted between the map sprawled out across his desk and the blank page staring back at him. How long had he been there, eyes jumping between the two? It was dark out, but then again, days and weeks had likely passed during his three way staring contest. Siuda was probably already in the East, shaking hands, kissing babies, and performing miracles, as he always was. Stepanov sighed. He knew his flight left in the morning, knew that there was so much work to do, but yet it was far easier to pace. And so he did. He paced. And paced. And paced.

Stepanov woke up three hours before his departure, the blank page continuing to mock him. Damn it all! Stepanov looked to the window, and the purple hue of the sky told him morning was soon to come. Slowly, Stepanov rose from the office chair he had made his bed, and walked to the window. He stood, arms folded behind him, and looked over the not-yet awake city. This was his domain. This he could handle. But far off in the horizon were many more obstacles to overcome, adventures to see to completion, and legacy's to lay. Stepanov could not help from smiling, that's why he did it. His grin grew larger. Siuda did it for the ideology, but Stepanov, Stepanov did it for the chase. For the pressure, for the glory.

Ivan Stepanov sat at his desk in the transitionary period between day and night. Though time may be indecisive, he would be no longer. Stepanov gripped his pen tightly around his fingers, and let the words flow out of the end until the once blank page was a detailed description of troop deployments and orders during his absence in Siberia. Problem areas, such as Tomsk and the Mongolian communes, would require additional men in his absence. Stepanov adorned the newborn order with his signature, surely they could keep things in order until he returned from the East.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.27.desc:
Igor had left his home at his usual time, in his usual clothes, and with the usual thoughts bouncing around his head. What would work be like today? What would he have for lunch? Would he be home before his kids fell asleep? And as Igor made his usual commute to the factory, a foreboding feeling began to envelop him. The usual routines of his neighbors were not in full swing, not on display for all to see. There was no smell of morning cooking. There were no children preparing for school. There was no life in the outskirts of Tomsk. Yet, a ferocious beating came from the town square, contrasted sharply by a mellow orchestra. It was unusual.

Pyotr had left his home at an early hour, in the thickest clothes he had, and with the most unusual thoughts bouncing around his head. Who all would be there? What were the chants again? Who was D.S? And as Pyotr made his unusual commute to the city center, it only took him three blocks until the butt of a firearm made contact with his face.

Mihkail had stepped off the train into Tomsk in the dead of night. He and 399 of his companions were to make a home of the city, joining the two thousand men already stationed in the days prior, per the orders of the highest military authority in Siberia. And as the men began to set up shop in the city, a sense of dread, that of being watched, crept up and over him. As night turned to day, and residents of the city of art awoke to the arrival of military personnel, he was sure there would be chaos.

Dimitri Shostakovich had left his hovel which functioned as both a hideout and prison, in the early hours of the morning, scarf wrapped haphazardly around his neck. To Dimitri, the morning was routine. Go early, collect what was needed, and return 'home' for another day of drinking. However, as Dimitri hobbled past the train station, and saw the train car let loose a flood of countless soldiers pour over the city, his mind had been made. Without delay, the old man spread like a virus, waking up his old allies in the city that once was his home, and prepared them to take to the streets to let their voices be heard.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.27.a: As dawn broke, Tomsk was a city on lockdown.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.28.desc:
Outside the repurposed Tomsk police station, temporary headquarters of the Black Army, the chants, marching of feet, and soft orchestral music of the protesters created the perfect soundtrack for the civil war raging in the Black Army.

Anarchism knows no borders, or, at least that's what they say. In truth, the anarchists had split themselves, and soon to be the entirety of the Free Territory in twine. A boundary had been established on each side of the barrack, nearly all 2,400 men taking up a side. On the left, ironically, stood those in concurrence with their orders. Opposite them, a big tent faction of those opposed to the deployment had taken shape. Words were their bullets, for now, and as arguments swelled, the tension continued to rise.

“You act like you don't know where we are!” Struggled one voice against the crowd, “This city is of artistic expression and cultural advancement, not war! I was there when Comrades Siuda and Stepanov marched down these same streets the protesters do, and I watched as-”

“Jesus, shut the hell up!” Retorted a voice from the other side, “You want to speak so highly of the reactionaries? Go join them. We are here to maintain the peace, this demonstration only proves General Stepanov correct. While our comrades wipe out the last remnants of statism in the East, it is our duty to keep order here.” Murmurs of agreement fought against the jeers of the Siudaists.

As the debate raged on, one man, a recent recruit to the Black Army, sat nervously by his radio. For hours, since the protests began, he had been desperately radioing out for someone to restore order. However, it became apparent that the Free Territory was nothing more than its biggest names. Without the leadership of Valenteev, the decisiveness of Mishurenko, nor the ideological conviction of Siuda, the Army was left directionless, and no amount of votes would iron the issue out. Mercifully, the radio crackled to life. After hours of trying, he was transferred to General Stepanov in his temporary eastern headquarters in Chita. “Comrade General, this is Pavel-”

“I don't care. You've made thirty attempts to reach me in the last hour. What is going on?”

“Protests, they've protesting for-” Somewhere behind him, glass shattered, and the voices of the two factions grew louder, “Comrade General, the people want us out and some of the men here agree, dozens have already joined the protesters. Please advise.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.28.a: Through gritted teeth, the General ordered a withdrawal.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.28.b: With much resolve, the General demanded a return to order in Tomsk.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.29.desc:
Ivan Stepanov paused for time he did not have. He had hardly even left Novosibirsk, and already the house of cards began to crumble. Through the receiver, he could hear it, the sound of all his plans unfolding. Damn it all. He thought back to the order, his final deployments made before he was due to depart for the East. If only he had worked a little harder, started a little sooner, planned even further ahead. The wave of possibilities crashed over him. With more vetting, he could've assured that his most loyal followers were in charge of the city. With more planning, he could've preempted any protests. With hindsight, things would be perfect.

“Comrade General?” The two simple words saved Stepanov from falling deeper down the pit of what-if. Stepanov pulled at his face, mulling over the decision. He made his home out of the old Tsar's palace, and from the grand balcony, Stepanov looked out. It was new and lawless and untamed. But it would never be his if the core of his power base collapsed. So what was he to do? Concede to the first sign of resistance? But if he couldn't keep Tomsk in order, how could he keep the East under his boot? But if-

“Comrade General? Please advise.”

Stepanov's eyes widened, right! There was no more time for indecisiveness. Stepanov took a deep breath, and through gritted teeth delivered the most difficult order, his second test. “Listen carefully. My orders are clear. You say that factions have arisen? There will be a complete reorganization of command structure. Half of you will remain at the city's outskirts. I will radio for General Mishurenko to prepare accommodations. The other half, those sympathetic to the agitators, are reassigned to patrols along the border to our south. I will radio to General Chapayev to open up his headquarters in Tuva for your arrival. Understood?”

“Yes, Comrade General.”

“One more thing,” Stepanov said, “As you leave, remember, this is not a walk of shame, nor the last time you'll see the city.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.29.a: “There will be no protests once I return.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.30.desc:
It started on the radio three decades ago. Dimitri Shostakovich; the best composer of his time! A visionary, a genius, a prodigy. Through those decades, those adjectives slipped into the background, kidnapped and replaced with new ones. A politician, a leader, a hero. Even then, he was not long for those titles either. As the anarchists of the Black Army moved north and into the city he had made his home since the fall of the Union, he became the antithesis of his younger self. A drunkard, a failure, a recluse. And for a time, it seemed as though those would be the last words to describe him. Passion fades, but talent doesn't. No matter what he did, Dimitri Shostakovich excelled in everything, even when he failed, he failed spectacularly, and he failed hopefully. Hopeful, even as Tomsk fell, that a new sun would rise over the city.

It started on the radio three hours ago. Stepanov's orders were clear. There would be no withdrawal, no capitulation to the protestors' demands for an end to the occupation. Soldiers exploded out of the building, two currents forking from one stem. One flowing to the side of the people and the protestors, and one to the opposite end of the city square. As men took their places for what would be the final symphony, and prepared for the crescendo, it was clear the winning side had already been predetermined. The protest was quickly organized, if it was even organized at all, and men, women, and children alike stood side by side with nothing more than their fists and their resolve and they knew they would lose. The soldiers, puppets of the scheming General, had lined up, prepared to carry out their orders, with reinforcements undoubtedly behind them. Dimitri Shostakovich watched, helpless, as his city split in two, for the third time in his life.

As David slayed Goliath, so too was the fragile peace slain by a single stone. Someone, from one side or the other, had let loose a rock, hurling it towards the other side. One rock became ten, and the voices of the soldiers grew louder, and the symphony hastily organized by the composer played louder to compensate, and anarchy ran wild like a river. As stones became bullets, Dimitri Shostakovich saw his city for the last time, in a fleeting glance, as sharp pain took root in his skull and spread outward like a virus. And as he lay dying, the music stopped, the chanting stopped.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.31.t: No Sleep on the Western Front
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.31.desc:
It was late, at least, to an old man. General Androniy Mishurenko stood, hands tightly clasped behind him, and looked out over the horizon, to the west. Though his face remained still, maintaining that same posie and stoic grace he had determined to carry himself with, his heart fought with his brain. And more recently, his brain had been losing. He yearned for the west, but with each passing day, the vision of his home became a little more blurry. Each night he spent on the frontier of the warlord states to the west, he thought about crossing over, simply stepping out of the Free Territory, and back into Sevastopol, to Moscow, to Leningrad, to home.

Mishurenko was literally shook from his thoughts as a small hand grabbed tight to him from behind. The old general turned, face distorted into a scowl, and prepared to let loose a lecture on properly attracting the attention of one's superior. Before he could, however, Mishurenko took a moment to size up who he was dealing with. A scrawny boy, one of thousands just like him, with desperation in his eyes. Mishurenko never had a son, or maybe he did, it had become hard for him to remember even the most important of details. But the look in the boy's eyes told him something was gravely wrong.

“Comrade General!” the boy cried, “A fight!” The boy bent over, hands resting on his knees, as he caught his breath. “These two men, I don't know their names, I'm sorry, I- well I just ran over immediately, someone told me to, I don't know their name either, I'm sorry, but two of the recent recruits, just like me, they, they started fighting. One is from Kansk, I know that much, said his father met Siuda, I mean Comrade Siuda, I'm sorry, personally! Anyways, another, the other guy, said something about a lack of resolve, how his father had served with Comrade General Stepanov and-”

Mishurenko raised his hand, bringing the frantic boy to silence. The night was quiet again, only the low wind indicating that the world continued to turn. The old general looked back west, towards all he fought for, and considered his situation carefully. He was well aware of the friction between the boy and Stepanov, but now, it was spreading to the Army. He would be damned if his work to return to home was stopped by petty politics. Mishurenko put a hand on the boy's shoulder, and looked him square in the eyes, “Thank you. I will deal with things from here.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.31.a: A rare glimpse of sanity from the mad general.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.32.desc:
“To: General Ivan Stepanov

As the most senior elected officer in the Black Army, I have seen many people come and go. You will recall that I was one of the first to attach myself to this movement, and I have spent those years since wondering if I made the wrong decision. As we froze in the Assembly Hall in Kansk, decades ago now, I watched as you built a kingdom around yourself, a Tsardom in the anarchy. I took notice of your actions, admittedly first falling victim to your tricks. For some time, I believe you were just as committed to this as Pyotr.

But as we grew out, expanded from bandits to statesmen, I saw you for who you were. You are a general, not an ideologue. Perhaps I am reading you wrong once again, but I believe there comes a time where we have to show our true selves. Last night, a fight broke out between two of my inferiors, torn apart by the politics you and the boy preach. It was then it was clear to me that you have grand plans for Russia, plans far beyond visiting the Far East out of goodwill.

As a military officer myself, I am perhaps biased in my decision on which horse to bet on in this race, in this struggle for power, but I believe I can lend you some valuable advice. What you have done to the Army and to the people of Russia at large is appalling, and still, I believe the worst is yet to come. However, it is in your best interest to know that you command plenty of respect, and you do not need me to tell you how much power you wield, but will never match the boy in terms of public popularity. I have led countless campaigns all across the carcass of the Union, and I have not once met a man equal to Pyotr Siuda in charm, nor resolve. If this is a battle you intend to win, you must drop any pretenses of winning on the battlefield of words.

Rumors have begun to spread in your absence and in Siuda's. Your misguided decision regarding the city of Tomsk speaks to this point. There have been whispers of further rebellion in Kemerovo, though I am unable to substantiate them. Likewise, I have gotten word from a contact in the Amur region that Siuda is to make a stop there in the coming days. This would provide a perfect opportunity to remove the issue once and for all, simply rid yourself of the boy then and there. I cannot tell you which decision to make, but I will say, if you intend to govern as a strongman, you must act like one.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.32.a: Eager to rid himself of the issue all together, Stepanov began drawing plans to assassinate Siuda.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.32.b: Still playing the long game, Stepanov began drawing plans to investigate the brewing protests in Kemerovo.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.33.desc:
Stepanov had read and re-read Mishurenko's letter over and over again. He paced, and read. As he laid in bed, he read. As he shook hands and laid the foundations of connections essential for a soon-to-be dictator, he repeated the letter again and again and again in his head. If he were to be a strongman, he'd need to act like one. The phrase echoed in his head, thrashing around wildly, denying him sleep, peace, and efficiency. As had become habit, after returning back to his temporary residence in the former Imperial Palace, Stepanov stood on the balcony, and looked out into the city, searching for the answer.

He hated himself. He had always been cool and composed, and a single letter had reduced him to an indecisive mess. Of course, that was only a persona, but he hoped that if he faked it hard enough, it would become him. That word had come to haunt him; indecisive. Everytime he thought he had successfully excised it from him, it came back. There were only so many times he could walk back and forth in his room, or lie wide awake in his bed, and push the issues out of his head. It became an attack on his pride. Mishurenko, the elderly and forgetful general, had the nerve to tell Stepanov what to do. Who does he think he is? Stepanov knew the answer to that question of course; he was someone who was right.

Stepanov looked to the east from the balcony, somewhere, Siuda was out there too. Instinctively, his hands had curled into fists. If he didn't do something, the boy would run Russia into the ground, leaving behind a legacy of weakness and rubble. There had been plenty of opportunities to kill the boy in the past, but none seemed right, everytime he hesitated, not out of friendship, but out of fear. Stepanov did not care for Siuda, but, in his heart of hearts, he was terribly afraid of him. The moment Stepanov became aware of that feeling, that Siuda could win, he knew what he had to do. The boy would die, and he would reign. He wasted no time in devising a plan, drafting a plan for his most dedicated and experienced men to await Siuda on the outskirts of his destination, while Stepanov returned to Central Siberia so as to provide himself an alibi.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.33.a: Our decisions ripple out, changing the future in their wake.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.34.desc:
Pyotr Siuda sat bored in his vehicle as it traversed the Russian landscape. The denazification project he had undertaken in what was once Rodzavesky's domain had been a resounding success, even if there had been one significant thorn in his side. Ahead of him, the vehicle carrying his personal guard bounced up and down against the terrain. To his rear, two other vehicles followed closely behind, one carrying Yevgeniya and other aides, and behind them the supply truck. Tired of being tired, Siuda leaned forward from the back seat, “Comrade,” Siuda addressed his driver, “Are we still on track to be in the city before midnight? We had planned to set up shop overnight and get to work right away in the morning.”

His driver nodded, “Yes.” Siuda smiled, a man of few words! He seemed to attract people like that, perhaps to compensate for his abundance of them. Content, Siuda leaned back in his seat, and let himself drift off to sleep, exhausted from his busy schedule.

Before his eyes opened, his head hurt. Siuda had found himself on the floor of the vehicle, sprawled out and face down. He could hear the engine roaring, and felt the sharp turns of the vehicle threaten to throw him around like a schoolyard ball. Gripping his seat tightly and pulling himself up, Siuda saw the earth move quickly around him. His brow furrowed as he looked out the windshield and saw no lights ahead of him. Siuda's brain began to race, almost matching the speed of the vehicle, was this a kidnapping? No, surely not, the two vehicles behind him would never allow it. Once more, Siuda leaned forward to the driver's seat, “What are you doing?!”

Eyes still focused on the road, the driver spoke calmly, “The vehicle ahead of us was ambushed,” The driver took his hands from the wheel to exaggerate his point, “men swarmed out of the woods, they had rifles, like this.” The driver mimed holding a firearm. “We have to get you out of here.” The driver returned his hands to the wheel and continued full speed ahead. Siuda leaned back in his seat for the second time, processing the situation. This wasn't a bandit attack, it was an assassation attempt. Although it was no secret many people wanted him dead, only one person had the resources to pull off an attack such as this one.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.35.desc:
In one hour and thirty-six minutes, it would be exactly twenty four hours since he departed from the Imperial Palace for the last time. That would mean that in one hour and thirty-five minutes ago, it would be twenty four hours since Pyotr Siuda was killed. Stepanov took deep, long, breaths. This was a good thing, he told himself. This was the decision of a strong man. After the thousandth time, he almost started to believe it, and the anxiety he felt started to slip away.

From his seat next to the window, Stepanov saw the expanse of Russia beneath him. Now, there was nothing in the way of his power play. He had already rehearsed his speech, that while working together with Siuda in the integration effort, a rogue member of the Russian Fascist Party attacked Siuda's vehicle, and Stepanov barely escaped with his life. The wheels turned in his head of just what would be his first move after taking Russia for himself. Dinner sounded nice.

Paranoid about his decision, Stepanov had demanded a report on the assassination as soon as it had been carried out. From the back of the plane came a soldier, a single sheet of paper in his hand. “Comrade General,” he saluted, “I just got word from the men on the ground regarding your...” the soldier cleared his throat, “operation.” The man presented the paper to Stepanov, who took it, and waved his hand so as to dismiss the soldier.

Stepanov hastily scanned over the document. Tracing the words with his finger as he read, Stepanov jumped between important words. Ambush. Siuda. Skirmish. Escape. Failure. Stepanov froze for a second on the final word, failure. Siuda had escaped unscathed, and more than likely clued into Stepanov's plans. Ivan tore the page in two and crumbled each half in his hands. He should've known there would be no easy solution for this problem. Assassins had failed him, but he wouldn't fail again. There was no other choice but to be a strong man now.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.35.a: He would have to do it himself.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.36.t: In the Court of the People's Prince
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.36.desc:
“I was born here.” Alexi gestured around him, “I'm telling you that one of the old generals from the Union totally lost the plot, declared himself king! My dad was literally there when Siuda told Rurik that he wasn't going to kill him.” Ivan, walking beside him, only rolled his eyes, as if. He was gullible, sure, he had fallen victim to a few pranks, but he wasn't stupid. The town didn't even look like a kingdom! It was shabby, there were no monuments to a king, there was no fanfare of a court, it just looked like the rest of Russia. “You still don't believe me?” Alexi asked, facing Ivan, “You will. The warehouse we're heading towards is supposed to be filled to the brim with old stuff from the kingdom. Guns, uniforms with the crown on it. You'll see.”

When they finally arrived at the warehouse, the sun had begun to set. Their elected officer had organized the company into two groups to cover each half of the facility. To Alexi's chagrin, the two were paired together, and began to sift through the boxes. Finding nothing of substance, Ivan stood triumphantly. “Told you. There's nothing here that proves there was ever a kingdom. I mean come on, you have to be a special type of stupid to thin-”

Without warning, the warehouse had turned pitch black. Conversation died out immediately, and silence fell over them all. For a moment, Ivan was sure he had gone blind, but only a moment later, the lights sprang back to life. In the center of the building, armed guards stood in a circular formation around a man adorned by a great, flowing, fur coat. The tension in the air was palpable, as confused glances were shared by the Black Army soldiers. “This is an illegal search,” The man bellowed, “and a clear violation of the people's rights. As such, a militia has surrounded the building to ensure the integrity of our belongings. All armed soldiers will depart from this area at once.” Ivan turned to Alexi, eyes wide and fixated on the man he recognized as Prince Yuiry. The Prince's back was to Ivan, and the two were in such a spot that they were unseen by the guards. Ivan's breath became shaky, and he looked to his firearm. Something came over him, something he could not control. He wrapped his trembling hand around the gun, aimed,
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.36.b: And dropped the gun to his side.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.37.desc:
Ivan had never shot a man before. It felt a bit like shooting a target, like he had been trained with. He was nervous, but this was what he had been trained for. It felt like he could watch the bullet fly through the air in slow motion, the world moving at a minute a second. He watched as one by one by one, people reacted to the noise. Then, he heard, one by ten, by hundreds, as the reality of the situation set in for them. The Prince, one of the last links to the Rurikid dynasty, joined his sister on that warehouse floor.

Alexi pulled Ivan down onto the cold floor in an instant. Alexi's eyes were wild, and his voice was hushed but frantic, “You shot him!” He panted, “You shot him!” Alexi repeated the phrase over and over again, but Ivan could hardly hear it as the sound of gunfire rang out all around him. Ivan kept his eyes wide open, afraid that if he closed them again he would see the Prince again. Alexi grabbed his shoulders, still flat on his belly, “You shot him, Ivan! Oh my God!” They didn't need to look to know that a massacre was taking place, but Ivan could not help but poke his head up and over their hiding spot. He saw the door in which they entered, the door to the outside world where this assignment was boring only minutes ago. The Prince wasn't bluffing. More men rushed in, loyalists to the crown, or to the city, and just as they came in, they fell.

For an eternity, the sound of gunfire and the smell of death hung in the air, smothering oxygen and keeping the two young soldiers firmly in place. Multiple times, the sound of firearms ceased, only to begin again, this time more ferocious. Finally, though, it let up for good, but Ivan didn't stand. Alexi did, however, and wept.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.38.desc:
Ivan's trembling hands let the gun fall loose, and drop to the floor. Alexi, reacting to the noise, looked between Ivan and the gun multiple times, dumbfounded. He yelled in a whisper, “Jesus! You were going to shoot him? Are you trying to get us all killed?” Ivan struggled to find the words, stuttering out some sort of explanation that he was just trying to defuse the situation before it began, and he was only following training, and he had never been in combat before, and a million other excuses that clogged his throat.

The elected officer had stepped forwards, hands off his weapon, and begun to quietly converse with the Prince. “We are just investigating a claim that this building is being used to house weapons and ammunition to bring down the Free Territory. We are fully within our rights, under clearance of the Security Council, to investigate and destroy pro-statist rebellions before they spring up.” The officer stepped closer to the Prince, eliciting a reaction from his guard, “If you, and the people of this city, have nothing to hide here, there is no reason to point weapons at us.”

The Prince shook his head and responded sternly, “You brought down this kingdom in the name of liberty and now you will trample on it for the possibility of safety?” The Prince crossed his arms defiantly, “The ultimatum is the same.”

Alexi turned to Ivan, “See, I told you I wasn't lying, there really was a kingdom here.” Alexi and Ivan watched as the officer and the prince exchanged remarks for what seemed like forever. Ivan had regained some of his composure but couldn't shake the feeling that he could've done something horrible. As they sat and waited, and waited, and waited, the soldiers on both sides grew more comfortable. Still on edge, but the slightest noise would not trigger a massacre. What they were all oblivious too was the growing number of civilians outside the warehouse. The Prince wasn't bluffing. By the time that the officer had stepped away from Yuiry, they had been outnumbered by the town's people and had no choice but to accept the Prince's demands. One by one, the soldiers filed out of the warehouse, empty handed, and marched out of Kemerovo in shame.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.38.a: Stepanov won't be happy to hear about this.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.39.t: Extra, Extra! Read All About it!
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.39.desc:
An editorial in The Revolutionary, a publication in Tomsk, by Viktor Nekrasov.

“What should've been a quiet night in Kemerovo was anything but. Without reason, or prior notice, one hundred soldiers marched into the city. Residents of Tomsk will be familiar with this story. Soldiers occupied a building, and when the community stood up against this blatant overreach and display of disregard for the values of anarchism, the Black Army stood in opposition to the people. Though the full story has not yet been discovered, it is speculated that the Army arrived, occupied, and opposed the people off a flimsy rumour of weapons smuggling. As we await further news ro trickle out of Kemerovo, we ought to take a step back and question why incidents such as these happen more and more frequently.

While I think some have always been suspicious of the power of the military, those individuals have been vindicated as of late. I encourage you to recall your memory of the latest assembly meeting you attended. How many guards were there? Then, think of the meeting before that and ask yourself the same question. With Comrades Valenteev and Mishurenko on opposite sides of the Free Territory, and Siuda and Stepanov in the East, the Black Army has been left to babysit us while Mother Anarchy and her many grooms are out.

The skirmishes in Tomsk and Kemerovo prove one thing, even if the Black Army has turned its back on liberty, the people have not. This pressure must be applied continuously and universally, squashing all facets of authoritarianism where they arise. What will you do when hundreds of soldiers march into your town? Will you stand up, or will you sit idly by as freedom dies. This state dressed in all black can not masquerade itself as an anarchist society. Question why, because for every troop deployment, or reshuffling of divisions, there is someone making that decision.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.39.a: When the journalists get hold of a good story, they never let it go.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.40.desc:
The Imperial Palace was many things. A home, a city center, a monument to all the unflinching resolve of the Russian people in the service of their Tsar. To Pavel, a peasant boy born to farmers in the Angra Basin, it was a dream, a place as real as Moscow, only alive in the past. As the hulking metal doors slammed shut behind him, Pavel awoke from his dream. The Imperial Palace was not a home, or anything like that now. Now, the palace was a graveyard. Empty. Save for the two last occupants. A peasant and a pretender.

Behind him, Pavel could still hear the cheers and the echoing boom of the comrade General's speech, and could still smell the ash of looted artwork, propaganda leaflets, and bodies burned. The view in front of him wasn't much better. The body of a man, crumpled and discarded like worthless scraps of paper, lied contorted on the ground, the remains of his glasses dangling from his face. If it were not for the subtle rises and falls in his chest, the man would be indistinguishable from a corpse. Pavel offered the man a sad smile. It was disturbing, but it was right, right? That's what he was supposed to see, he was a soldier, an anarchist!

“A peasant.” The soft voice from the man below him brought Pavel out of his trance. “They've sent a peasant to dispatch me.” The man laughed, a laugh that quickly devolved into a cough, and then to a weeze. Pavel watched in silence as the heap of a man began to take shape, and rose to his knees. The two met eyes. “Aren't you? You are not noble. You are a boy.”

Pavel took a deep breath, and felt his hand drift towards his side arm. He was right. He was just a boy.

“What have I done to deserve this? To die on my knees to a peasant? The rest were executed before the people, backdropped by roaring speeches and displays of military force!” The pretnder's words echoed out throughout the hollow building, prompting Pavel to draw his weapon and plant it against his prisoner's forehead as instructed, “This is not justice, nor liberty. You will soon find out that you are on the side of tyranny.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.40.a: A bullet does not care for family lineage.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.41.desc:
“Wait a few meters north. You'll see me when I'm done,” Stepanov instructed, waving off his guards as he stepped out from his vehicle. The engine, once dead, sprang to life, and light emerged from the front of the truck, the only light to be found. The brief illumination offered Stepanov a chance to truly observe his surroundings; snow, trees, and snow and trees. The only sign of civilization came from the dilapidated hovel before him. Incredible, he scoffed, what special breed of idiot would fight for this? The press of rubber against snow became audible as the light emanating from behind ceased to be. Stepanov took a deep breath, surely taking in more frost than oxygen, and adjusted his cap. This had better be worth it.

Before he could even reach the entrance, the door swung open, and out hobbled an elderly man, clearly missing an eye and certainly missing brain cells. “General!” The man spoke with reverence, despite the two never having met, “It's an honor to host you, please, come in.” The old man turned on his heel and marched back into his Siberian shack, with Stepanov a safe distance behind. Immediately, the familiar stench of mildew crashed over him like a wave. It didn't take long for him to find the source; scattered all across the floor were folders, documents, and loose papers. Though the bureaucrat in Stepanov cringed at the organization of what could only be critical information, his intrigue trumped his compulsivity as his eyes drifted past the swastika stamped atop each one.

“Don't want to be seen out of the city with those!” The old man teased, “Even then, word is your friend intends to visit Rodzaevsk.”

Stepanov scowled at the very notion he would ever befriend the bumbling moron espousing his nonsense. “Indeed. I'm sure you are less than enthusiastic about that. I don't imagine he's there to erect a memorial to the late Vozhd.”

The old man flashed a devilish grin and let loose a hearty laugh. “Just as enthusiastic as you are, General!” The old man plopped into a wooden chair, hardly able to support his weight, and gestured for Stepanov to do the same. “Scattered around you is my life's work, every single document regarding the Russian Fascist Party, it's members, operations, invaluable information for someone seeking to set up shop in this neck of the woods.”

Stepanov gestured his hands outward, “So you said in your letter. I hardly believe this is a gift of goodwill from a fascist to a man such as myself. What's your catch?”

“What do you think? I want what you want!” The man leaned in much closer, stomach over the table, inches away from Stepanov's face, “I expect my slice of Siberia too.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.41.a: Maybe he wasn't as stupid as Stepanov thought...
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.42.desc:
Magadan was not one city, but two. Not in the way of Buda and Pest, although thinking of the Magyar capital did arouse a sardonic smile in the aging Romanian. No, the difference between the two Magadans was quite simple; one was completely fictional. Everyone west of the city imagined it as a modern day Venice, the weak, but still beating, heart of Russia. Sure, foreign goods made the city more liveable than most, but what was a pile of shit to a heap? Perhaps he was a bit too hard on the city, afterall, it had served as home for the better half of a decade. There had to be something magic to keep a mercancy in one spot.

It was late, some hour between dark and very dark, but even the cloud coverage could not blot out the light beckoning him towards the tavern on the hill. He smiled. There was the magic! Gripping a gloved mitten tightly around the handle, the Romanian threw open the door and stepped into the warmth of company.

The bar was nearly empty, physically. However, the bombastic personalities of the occupants certainly compensated. “Well look what the cat dragged in!” came one voice, accent weighing heavily over the r's. The Romanian smiled as he removed his coat, hanging it up against the wall. “Best come take a look at this one! Never have I seen an offer like this before!” The Romanian made his way to the roundtable of the knights of WerBell, and took a seat. At the table's center, a stack of papers had been neatly compiled. The Romanian furrowed his brow, his compatriots watching on as he picked up one from the top of the stack and scanned over it. At the top there were big, red, letters, incomprehensible to the Romanian.

“That one's mine.” A nimble hand snatched the paper out of the Romanian's. “Cyrlic, but the language is French.” The Romanian's eyes fell back to the table, and as he pawed through the other pages, he made a final tally. One in French, one in Romanian, two in English.

“That general. Monsieur... Stepanov? Yes. His offers are...how you say, rather high.”

“Aye,” said the voice across the table, “but it strikes me as sketchy. Even Nancy walked away from it, got another offer from another lady associated with the general.” The man took a swig of his drink, “But those numbers...I'd be happy to share that with ye, anarchism be damned.”
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.43.desc:
Chernov had always been a man of duty, unflinching dedication to his country and to the cause in which he believed defining his life from the moment he entered this world. For as long as he could remember, the NKVD had been all he had ever known. They had taught him right from wrong, who to kill and what it meant to do so, and of great revolution. He had come to accept this, even as his old comrades faded away beneath the boot of a new regime, a new face to sway the hand and call the people into the fervor of endless revolt.

Of course he had seen this all before, endless nights had been spent crouched inside musty offices, small talk absent beneath the flowing waves of the commonality they had all shared, revolution. To Mikhail Chernov, his sworn lifelong commitment to the protection of the revolution and all that accompanied it was the burning fire in his soul, a flame that kept the frigid cold of a bitter reality from seeping into his very person.

This shell shattered suddenly, a thunderous knock from his door shattering the relative silence of his domicile, muffled rasps echoing from just beyond the battered entrance as the dreams of past crumbled into a dreadful present. His nostalgia dissolved into a bubbling pit of despair and panic, sweat forming beneath his brow as the sweltering heat inside him screamed into a roaring flame of regret. Panic turned to action, and the vanguard stood from his desk, pausing as he considered rifling through its drawer in search of something to defend himself with.

Moving forward, Chernov seemed to almost stumble across the ragged wooden floorboards, the incessant creaks of wood stricken with rot filling the room as his hand trembled ever onward towards the doorknob. Palm slick with sweat, he fumbled attempting to turn it, eventually sticking his grasp upon the brass and curling his wrist downward, letting the door slam inward at his side.

And instead of the flash of a handgun, like the former operative had expected, a letter was extended up to his face, its pale white hue dotted with an almost obnoxious red seal.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.43.a: The revolution calls you, my friend.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.44.desc:
“For the time it took to get here, it sure wasn't worth it.” The old military man murmured, a certain venomous distaste lacing his every word as the grimace present upon his face exaggerated into a pained expression. It had been a long trip, Buryatia but another stop on the long road to control, and Stepanov had hoped that he would at least gain something more substantial from his visit. Despite his hopes, the reception in the region had been relatively cold, the people of Buryatia had not shown any interest in almost anything he had to say to them.

His fiery passion and iron fisted rhetoric had done nothing to save him from the cold blank stares he had received from the majority silent crowd, his oratory confidence dashed in a matter of minutes as the assembled gave not even a singular clap at the conclusion of his raving. He felt it all, the shame, the disdain, the confusion, it compounded upon him like a stack of tumbling bricks, rolling into an ever bigger feeling of innate despair at his rather public mishandling of his audience.

Though, as the almost suffocating embarrassment cast itself over the Black Army's guiding hand, he felt a twinge of pride in what he had accomplished. He had managed, despite the delays and suspicious hiccups in his travel, to beat Siuda to the punch, and that mattered. There was nothing he would love more than to thumb it in that anarchist's face, but it would take more than a few quick trains to rub Siuda's nose in the mud.

A resolve gripped him, the liquor he now swirled within the glass at his fingertips assisting in the calming of his frazzled nerves, stoic demeanor re-emerging as he pondered where his travels would take him next.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.45.desc:
Ivan felt the frigid air whip against his thick coat as he trudged through the snow ridden streets of Olomon, shuddering at nature's sting as his eyes swirled back and forth in desperate search of somewhere to hide away from the blistering wind. To his relief, albeit after a hushed prayer for safety and guidance slipped between his chattering teeth, the local drinking hole had not yet locked its doors to patrons. Almost sprinting forward, his legs wobbling upon the ice as he scrambled toward his salvation, he thought back to the purpose for which he had been sent here for.

Getting called into Stepanov's office was never usually a good thing, and in this case nothing was different. Dread filled him as soon as he pushed open the door, the stench of smoke and liquor filling his lungs as he took a seat before the Marshall. It had been a simple task, another brilliant scheme to undermine the assembly, Siuda especially, in this particular instance. He was promised extra pay, so he had taken it.

Stepanov, in all of his combined genius, had suggested that he travel to Olomon, a rather determinedly religious region in Central Siberia, and decry the anarchist as vehemently atheist. Ivan had laughed in the confines of his own thoughts when that was proposed to him, but the deathly serious look upon his commander's face made him reconsider the hilarity of the idea.

This was all in the past of course, right now Ivan was surrounded by infatuated locals, a nervous lilt in his voice as he rambled on and on about the demented evils of the anarchist and his hatred for god and his teachings. He had never expected it to go so well, but had nevertheless continued onward in his quest for Stepanov, fabricating and exclaiming as much profound knowledge on the atheist leanings of anarchism for all of Olomon to hear.

And as figures in the crowd stared up at him, nodding in what he could only assume was approval, Ivan silently released his breath, exhaling with great relief.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.46.t: With Apathy, From One General to Another
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.46.desc:
Amidst the columns of marching men, the thunderous booms of the band, and the cheers of loyal citizens, a very apathetic General Ivan Stepanov stood, the marching of boots setting the tempo of his pounding headache. Though outwardly he put on his best stoic look of valor, he was tired. His eyes, half glazed over, weakly drifted from person to person, meeting only the bare minimum required of a leader. How does Siuda do it? Always chipper, optimistic, and quick to unleash a tirade of horseshit. A thought crossed his mind, even for just a moment, that perhaps this wasn't worth it, that maybe he wasn't cut out to lead. Mercifully, a tight grip on his shoulder expelled that thought from him.

“Comrade General!” Thundered a deep voice, “It is an honor to meet with you!” Stepanov snapped to attention, quickly drinking in the situation. Before him, a ginormous bearded man stood, built like a tree stump. Behind him, men just like him stood in a V-formation, branching out from the biggest and the burliest. “You are a subject of much respect to us, especially in this city.” Ah, the memories came flooding back to Ivan, the protests. How he wished he was just as quick to forget.

Extending his hand out to the soldier, Stepanov found his footing in politicking once more, “The honor is my own. Neither of us would be standing here if the mob had had its way with the city.” Stepanov turned back towards the city square, towards the radio tower which marked the final destination of the siege of Tomsk all those years ago. “The situation was difficult, and only the best could've handled it as you did.” Behind the General, as if on cue, stepped forward two men with thick wooden boxes in tow. The boxes flipped open, revealing dazzling medals. Stepanov plucked one from its container and pinned it to the man's chest.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.46.a: Even Stepanov can share the credit.
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.47.t: With Love, From One General to Another
strings.SBA_PowerStruggle.47.desc:
“A drink?” Stepanov sipped from a foreign liquor, an imported item from his personal collection. “No doubt that the last few weeks have just as stressful for you as they have been for me.”

“No. I had my last drink in Sevastopol and I won't have another until.” Mishurenko uttered coldly, his arms crossed flatly across his chest.

Stepanov nodded as he drank from his glass, “Ah, I should've suspected. I take it you still haven't smoked then?” Mishurenko simply shook his head and kept his eyes fixated on Stepanov's. In turn, Stepanov raised an eyebrow, “Something nagging at you, general? I believe I'm familiar with you enough now to know this behavior, this silence, is unlike you.”

“What are you doing?” Asked the aging general, “Is this some sort of attempt to court me to your brewing coup?”

Stepanov flashed a cocky smile, “I won't insult your intelligence, general, it's no secret that the winds of change have only grown more ferocious. Though I must dispel the rumor of a hostile takeover.” The room fell to silence as Stepanov calculated his next words, “Androniy,” Stepanov steepled his hands across the table, “do you remember what I said to you, all those years ago, in Kansk? About loyalty? About our similarities?”

“Do you remember what I said in my letter?” Mishurenko spat the words, letting them fly freely across the table, “I am not your dog.” Stepanov opened his mouth to speak but was silenced. “Don't think for a moment that you have pulled the wool over my eyes once more. Your schemes have sown factionalism and distrust among the Black Army. It's no secret where your loyalties lie, General Stepanov.” Mishurenko turned away, “And the same is true for myself.”

“I'm not asking for anything but your support. I want to bring the Germans to heel, I want revenge, I want justice.” A devious grin crept across Stepanov's face, “I want you to smoke again.”

The old man's face scrunched together as if the words he had been fed were spoiled and rotten. He rose, and looked down upon the fat General sitting at his desk, “You may think that you're the only thing keeping this project together, but you're wrong. The time after the boy is gone will be tumultuous,” Mishurenko turned to the door, wrapping a wrinkled hand around the knob.
